summary: Redwood AE/SE ran an edge-case demo for BlueHeron focusing on very long context sessions (~200k tokens), sustained high TPS bursts, streaming response backpressure, and timeout/fallback strategies. Discussion covered batching, KV cache eviction, per-session TTLs, circuit-breaker policies, Dedicated capacity vs hosted fallbacks, and concrete next steps to run benchmarks with customer traces.
topics: Dedicated vs Hosted routing and fallbacks
questions: How does Redwood handle KV cache eviction for long sessions?
What happens to a streaming connection when worker hits OOM?
Can we pin sessions to Dedicated pool and fallback to hosted with data residency constraints?
transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-11-20 15:00 PST
- Duration: 52 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Arjun (Redwood SE), Elena (BlueHeron), Tom (BlueHeron), Priya (BlueHeron), Jamal (BlueHeron SRE)

[00:00] Maya: okay, hi everyone thanks for joining, we're going to walk through the long context + high t p s playbook, and then run a couple of live scenarios. quick check—anyone who needs to leave early?
[00:08] Elena: no, good to go. excited, we burned through some of the doc last week but haven't seen the live behaviors.
[00:12] Liam: cool, I'll start with how we model long sessions, and then we'll show an example of streaming backpressure and the timeout policies we recommend. bear with me, i might use shorthand for some infra bits.
[00:23] Tom: fair, and i'll pipe in with the platform constraints we have — kubernetes autoscaler limits and our queueing infra.
[00:28] Arjun: quick note, we put the playbook on the shared drive: "redwood/edgeplaybooks/long-context-backpressure.pdf" (link).

---

[02:12] Liam: first, long context — typical failure mode is unbounded kv cache growth. if you're holding 100k tokens per session, naive approach fills GPU memory or triggers eviction that causes huge recompute. our runtime keeps an LRU-style segment map, and we recommend one of two patterns: session sharding (split very long conversations into pinned prefixes + active window) or offloading less-frequently accessed KV pages to CPU-backed storage with async prefetch. both have tradeoffs.
[02:43] Jamal: when you say offload, do you mean it stalls generation? our SLI is 500ms p95, anything above is a breach.
[02:52] Liam: good question. in the offload model you get a higher tail for cold fetches — maybe 200-600ms extra on those tokens — but you can keep steady throughput. that's why we pair it with adaptive batching and TTLs; we also recommend setting per-session priority: low priority sessions can be asynchronously served with a longer tail.

[04:10] Elena: and for us, many sessions are analytic transcripts that often go back months. we can't drop history.
[04:17] Maya: right — that's the scenario where we suggest pinning historical context in object storage and only materializing the most recent N tokens to GPU. the API supports on-the-fly partial context injection so you can synthesize the prompt window without blowing memory.

[05:00] Tom: what about streaming responses? our UI progressively displays tokens, and we saw earlier a case where streams freeze mid-response when our worker saturates.
[05:09] Liam: that's the backpressure case. when worker CPU/GPU queue hits saturation, internal queues fill and the streaming loop can block. Redwood has a multi-tier approach: 1) continuous batching so short responses don't sit behind huge batches, 2) per-connection token rate limiting, and 3) graceful partial sends — if a worker is about to OOM or time out, it'll send the partial output and flag the session as truncated with an explicit reason code in the response trailer.
[05:42] Priya: is that flag exposed to the client? we need to show 'response incomplete' in UI so product can decide to re-request or show fallback.
[05:49] Arjun: yup, trailer contains reason codes like EVT_TRUNCATED_BACKPRESSURE or EVT_TIMEOUT_FALLBACK, and also contains a resume_cursor you can use when you re-open the session. sometimes the transcript index mapping is imperfect — speech-to-text like we saw earlier — but the resume token works at the token boundary level.

[07:10] Jamal: okay, but if the worker sends partial and then dies, won't we lose the KV state?
[07:18] Liam: we persist checkpoints at regular intervals; worst case you lose the last few tokens worth of session metadata, not the entire history. for strict durability customers we recommend Dedicated pools with synchronous checkpointing to KMS-backed object store.

[08:50] Elena: Dedicated thing—cost is a concern. we want predictable latency but not commit to a full cluster unless necessary.
[08:58] Maya: totally—most customers use a hybrid: pin critical routes to Dedicated for low-latency SLA, and route bulk or exploratory workloads to hosted with a fallback policy. we can autoscale Dedicated with a minimum baseline to keep p95 low. pricing options are in the doc i'll send.

[10:15] Tom: about timeouts—what's the recommended client-side timeout vs server-side? we saw timeouts at 30s during spikes.
[10:24] Liam: we usually recommend client-side short timeouts for interactive flows (8-12s) and a server-side soft timeout at ~25s that sends a partial with EVT_TIMEOUT_FALLBACK; then a hard timeout at 45-60s depending on model/sequence length that is non-retryable. for batch jobs you can increase these. streaming complicates it because you want to keep the connection open for partial tokens.

[12:00] Priya: what about replays? can we replay the last 1k tokens into a faster model for quick summarization when timeout occurs?
[12:08] Arjun: yes — we call that model cascading: route to a smaller quantized variant for resume/summary. Redwood Optimize can suggest model candidates and quantization profiles based on your workload.

--- Live demo setup

[14:30] Liam: demo plan — i'll spin a simulated client that: 1) opens 200 concurrent sessions with 50k token prefixes, 2) issues a sustained 1,200 t p s burst for 30s, 3) simulates some random connection stalls to test partial sends. logging enabled.
[14:50] Tom: note — our prod-like traces are in the shared folder, i'll drop two example traces now.
[14:59] Tom: done. links: traces/blueheron/long-202611-trace.json

[16:05] Liam: starting run now...
[16:15] [30s into test] Liam: okay we see the front-door load balancer queueing, a small bump in latency at 95th, and two workers hit their kv-cache threshold and started offloading pages. one session shows EVT_TRUNCATED_BACKPRESSURE at 00:00:26.
[16:40] Priya: the UI shows a freeze at 00:26 — but the resume token is there. good.
[17:10] Liam: moving to the second step — we'll escalate to a host fallback for low priority sessions. toggling policy now.
[17:30] [policy change] Liam: routing switched, low priority sessions now sent to hosted fallback; p95 for high-priority pinned sessions improved by ~240ms.
[18:05] Jamal: what about the burst behavior — do you recommend smoothing client-side or letting runtime handle bursts?
[18:12] Arjun: both. smoothing upstream reduces peak ooms. on the runtime side we also support token-budget throttles at ingress with a burst window. the combination is most predictable.

[20:00] Elena: can Redwood surface which sessions are being offloaded so we can mark them differently in our UX?
[20:08] Maya: yes, Console has a per-session tag and stream of events. you can filter by reason code and assign SLO tiers. we can demo that in Console next week.

[22:30] Tom: i noticed one worker got an OOM and restarted — what happens to the stream in that case?
[22:38] Liam: the restart path attempts best-effort partial flush; if that's not possible the connection is closed with EVT_WORKER_RESTART and the resume cursor is still present if the checkpoint had been flushed. if not, we return a soft error and recommend retry with last-known checkpoint you stored client-side.

[24:50] Priya: any recommendations for client-side heuristics? like if we get EVT_TRUNCATED_BACKPRESSURE, should we immediately re-request with smaller context?
[24:59] Arjun: yes: 1) retry policy: backoff 200ms + jitter, 2) if repeated EVT_TRUNCATED_BACKPRESSURE reduce requested token window by 30% and prefer streaming=false for short summaries, 3) consider switching to a quantized model for immediate resume.

[27:10] Maya: quick security note — for BlueHeron with PII you can enable private deployment or VPC private control plane. dedicated pools can be configured for customer-managed keys. i'll attach the security excerpt.

[28:33] Elena: sounds good. for compliance we need audit logs showing which session had which reason codes for the past 90 days.
[28:41] Liam: Console exposes audit logs and per-request metadata; we can increase retention in the enterprise plan or stream logs to your S3.

[31:00] [wrap up demo] Liam: summary of what we saw — backpressure triggers partial sends with reason codes; offload + session sharding prevents OOM at expense of tail latency; Dedicated pinning reduces p95 significantly; fallback routing helps keep high-priority traffic healthy during bursts.
[31:24] Maya: next steps we agreed: we'll run a 2-hour bench with your traces next Tue; we'll provide a stress config and the streaming backpressure playbook; we'll also send pricing for a hybrid Dedicated baseline.

[32:10] Elena: sounds good. Jamal, Tom, any red flags from infra side?
[32:18] Jamal: nothing blocker. need to validate our autoscaler knobs though.
[32:23] Tom: we'll provide traces and quota requests by EOD Thursday.

[33:00] Priya: one last question — are there known edge cases where resume cursor fails?
[33:07] Arjun: rare cases when checkpoint didn't persist because of a storage write error; that's why we recommend client-side local checkpointing for critical flows, and dedicated sync for strict durability. we also emit a diagnostic id in the trailer so you can map to logs.

[35:00] Maya: piling on the action items: we'll share the playbook and the sample load script. Liam will lead the bench run with your engineers.

[36:10] [closing] Elena: great, thanks all. excited to run the bench.
[36:15] Maya: thanks everyone, we will follow up with calendar invite for the bench and links to docs. bye!
